records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name to put in the structured lead field, not on which names are right. RHS's dedicated Dicentra eximia page gives 'fringed bleeding heart' as its lead common name, in the plant-profile subtitle beneath the botanical-name H1 and in the page title 'Dicentra eximia (Ker Gawl.) Torr. | fringed bleeding heart', filing 'plumy bleeding heart, staggerweed, turkey corn' under a secondary 'Other common names' field. NC State Extension's dedicated page lists 'Bleeding-heart' first among its Common Name(s) (before 'Fringed Bleeding Heart' and 'Wild Bleeding Heart'), and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder displays 'Common Name: bleeding heart' as its lead, with fringed bleeding heart, plumy bleeding heart, staggerweed and turkey corn also carried in its Common Names list. Two of the three dedicated single-species sources (NC State, MoBot) lead with 'bleeding heart', but that name already belongs to Lamprocapnos spectabilis in this catalog, so common_name is 'Fringed Bleeding Heart' -- RHS's lead name, and the one all three sources attest. All three sources attest 'fringed bleeding heart', two of them in running prose: MoBot's description opens 'Dicentra eximia, commonly called fringed bleeding heart', and NC State's own Description opens 'Fringed bleeding heart is a beautiful, native perennial plant'.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's "Poisonous to Humans" block for Dicentra eximia rates Poison Severity as Low. Poison Part is listed in full as Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Seeds, Stems (no Roots listed for this species). Poison Symptoms, given in full: "Trembling, staggering, vomiting, diarrhea, convulsions, labored breathing if eaten in large quantities. Skin irritation after repeated contact with the cell sap is mild and short-lasting." Poison Toxic Principle is "Several isoquinolone alkaloids." (the page's own spelling, with a stray trailing character). Causes Contact Dermatitis is marked Yes. NC State also carries 'Poisonous' as a Whole Plant Traits > Plant Type value, lists 'Poisonous to Humans' as the sole entry under Problems, tags the page #poisonous, and banners 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' This Poison block is explicitly scoped to humans (headed "Poisonous to Humans"); the page carries no separate Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags, and RHS's and Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated pages carry no toxicity statement of any kind for this species, so no cat- or dog-scoped toxicity evidence was found among admissible sources -- only silence, not disagreement.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. NC State's dedicated page title/H1 bundles three names alphabetically as "Crested Iris, Dwarf Crested Iris, Iris," putting "Crested Iris" first. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder instead gives a dedicated single Common Name field reading "dwarf crested iris," and RHS's dedicated page carries "dwarf crested iris" as its primary plant-profile common name (its title reads "Iris cristata | dwarf crested iris"), with "lady's calamus" relegated to Other common names. Since two of the three dedicated single-species pages (MoBot and RHS) lead with "dwarf crested iris," that name is used as common_name here.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's "Poisonous to Humans" block (a human-scoped severity heading) rates Iris cristata's poison severity as Low, with poison symptoms: "Nausea, salivation, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, lethargy, elevated temperature following ingestion; skin irritation upon contact with seeds, rootstock, or cell sap. It causes only low toxicity if eaten. Skin irritation lasts for a few minutes. Highest concentration in rhizomes." Its poison toxic principle is "Pentacylic terpenoids (zeorin, missourin and missouriensin), Irisin, iridin, or irisine." The full poison part list is Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds -- never truncate this to fewer parts. NC State separately tags the plant with a "Contact Dermatitis" designation. Distinct from that human-scoped severity rating, NC State's Problems tag list carries its own "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" tags -- these are the basis for toxic_to_pets=true, since they name both cats and dogs specifically. RHS separately states a handling warning and an unscoped pet caution: "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants." RHS's "Pets" line does not itself name cats or dogs, so it corroborates but does not independently establish toxic_to_pets; that determination rests on NC State's separate cat- and dog-specific tags.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Poison block (human-scoped) rates Hydrastis canadensis as low severity: "CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, nervousness, and depression." The toxic principle is isoquinoline alkaloids, and the plant does not cause contact dermatitis. The full poison-part list covers the whole plant: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. This rating is scoped to humans only (NC State's page shows "Poisonous to Humans" under Problems, and lists no separate Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags for this species). Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder adds an unscoped whole-plant warning: "All parts of the plant are poisonous in large doses, however." NC State additionally carries "Poisonous" as a Whole Plant Trait and tags the species #poisonous, with the page header "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." The two sources differ in scope (NC State human-only, MoBot unscoped), and neither addresses cats or dogs, so no admissible source confirms or rules out toxicity to cats or dogs specifically. Both NC State Extension and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder independently describe the crimson/scarlet berry fruit as inedible, with no disagreement on this point.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets is left null: the only admissible toxicity evidence found (NC State Extension's Poison block) is explicitly scoped to humans, with no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags present on the Hydrastis canadensis page, and no other admissible source (Clemson HGIC, EDIS/ask.ifas.ufl.edu, RHS, Penn State, UMD, UGA fieldreport) was found to address cat- or dog-specific toxicity for this species.

water_regime is left null: Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field reads 'Water: Medium' (a mid-scale value that per the rules cannot support keep_moist), and no admissible source supplied a species-specific WATERING statement rather than a habitat-moisture or soil-adjective description, so no water_regime value could be assigned. The MoBot 'Water: Medium' figure is noted here as a disclosed counterpoint.

No dedicated schema field captures conservation/wild-harvest status, but it is decision-relevant: Penn State Extension states goldenseal's 'over-collection has reduced the population to dangerously low levels in many states' and that it was added to CITES Appendix II in 1997, and NC State Extension notes it 'has been listed as endangered or of special concern in North Carolina.' Both are admissible-source statements worth surfacing even though the schema has no field for them.

RHS's Hydrastis canadensis page lists Name Status as 'Unresolved' rather than 'Correct,' so scientific_name_accepted was instead supported via Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated species page binomial per the rules' alternative path.

The RHS page for this species returned only a common-name list and basic taxonomy; its Position/Cultivation/toxicity sections were not populated with content, so RHS could not supply light, soil, moisture, or toxicity data for this record.

No admissible source gave day/night temperature ranges, a chill-damage onset temperature (only USDA hardiness zone 3a-8b survival ratings were found, which per the rules are not onset temperatures), humidity percentages, foot-candle light values, or fertilizer interval/strength data for this species, consistent with it being an outdoor woodland perennial rather than a houseplant typically reported with such figures.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: Penn State Extension gives a percent-shade figure ('60 to 80 percent shade on more ideal sites') rather than a direct-sun-hours figure, and NC State's 2-6 hour figure comes from its site-wide Light-category legend, which the rules exclude as a source for this field.

soil_base is set to garden_bed as the closest available enum value for an in-ground woodland perennial grown directly in forest-floor/bed soil (per Penn State Extension's cultivation description); none of the potting-mix-oriented enum values (standard_potting, chunky_aroid, cactus_succulent, etc.) apply to this species.
